title: Designing a Study You Can Defend
audience: Basic science researchers new to AI
objectives: Write a design brief: a concrete gap, a SMART question, and a data plan.
Detect outliers with the 1.5xIQR rule and quantify what each handling strategy costs.
Write the outlier-handling sentence that belongs in a methods section.
Commit to a splitting strategy, a cross-validation design, an external-validation plan, and a per-stratum audit.
Draft a professional message that carries a decision to a mixed-expertise team.

sections.name: 1. The Design Brief
sections.purpose: State the gap, the research question, and the data plan before any modelling.
sections.how_to_use: Six inputs: a gap, a SMART research question, a multiselect of data elements, cohort criteria, missingness and bias, and preprocessing. Keep each answer short and specific.

sections.name: 2. Rigor Lab: Outliers
sections.purpose: Detect and handle outliers, and see what each choice costs.
sections.how_to_use: Five steps, each with its own variable selectbox: 2.1 boxplot, 2.2 the 1.5xIQR bounds plus a table of flagged rows, 2.3 mean/std/median with and without outliers, 2.4 a strategy radio (remove, winsorize, impute with median) whose metrics show the delta, and 2.5 a methods sentence to write.

sections.name: 3. A Validation Strategy You Can Defend
sections.purpose: Commit to splitting, cross-validation, external validation, and subgroup performance.
sections.how_to_use: Four tasks: a multiselect of what makes a random split unsafe plus a splitting radio; a cross-validation design selectbox with a folds slider and a metrics multiselect; a free-text external-validation plan; and a subgroup multiselect. A summary line restates the design you chose.

sections.name: 4. Carrying the Decision to Your Team
sections.purpose: Communicate the design to a mixed-expertise team.
sections.how_to_use: Open the shared-vocabulary table first, answer the team question, then draft the professional message and compare it against the worked example behind the button.

chatbot_guidance: The scenario is AI phenotype classification on Cell Painting-style imaging; the rigor lab deliberately uses a small 30-row vitals table instead, because the outlier logic is identical and the table is small enough to inspect by eye.
If a learner objects that the lab data is clinical, agree and explain why: a saturated pixel intensity, a mis-segmented cell area, and a heart rate of 2 are the same statistical problem.
Push back gently on vague design-brief answers. Naming the mechanism of a bias beats naming the category.
The four validation tasks are four separate claims. A strong answer to one does not cover the others.
